newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Jiang-Clinton talks positive -- Chinese spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Jiang-Clinton talks positive -- Chinese spokesman.

text.p: The meeting between Chinese President Jiang Zemin and U.S. President Bill Clinton on Sunday was friendly, positive and constructive, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said.
"President Jiang Zemin and President Clinton held very friendly talks. The atmosphere of the talks can be categorised as friendly, positive and constructive," Shen told a news briefing.
He said both presidents had agreed that their meeting on the sidelines of the APEC conference here was very important for Sino-U.S. relations and for their further development.
They are both attending the annual meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. They last met at the first APEC summit hosted by Clinton in Seattle in 1993.
They agreed to exchange state visits in 1997 and 1998 but the precise sequence and timing would be worked out through diplomatic channels.

U.S. Vice-President Al Gore would visit China early next year, however, for talks with Premier Li Peng on issues of mutual interest that would include environmental protection and energy cooperation, Shen said.
He said the two presidents had agreed there were still some issues, including trade problems, between the two countries, but they would settle them through constructive dialogue.

Shen said the atmosphere in their bilateral relations had improved, especially following the visit to Beijing earlier this month by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, during which some issues had been resolved.

Asked whether nuclear non-proliferation had been raised, Shen said the Chinese side had stressed its consistent attitude on the issue. It "has not, does not and will not" support weapons proliferation in any region.
He added the United States itself should adhere to the non-proliferation pact and agreements contained in three Sino-U.S. communiques by not exporting advanced weapons to Taiwan.
On China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), Shen said both presidents agreed "a pragmatic and flexible attitude should be adopted by both sides".
He said that a U.S. bid for a global agreement on free trade in computer and telecommunications technology and products, a contentious issue at the APEC talks so far, had not come up.
Shen said the issue of human rights had come up and "both sides agreed the question should be solved through dialogue, not confrontation".

He said Jiang and Clinton also discussed the Korean issue and expressed their hope that stability could be maintained on the Korean peninsula. Both sides could play a constructive role in supporting measures to foster stability there.

On U.S. concerns over the future of Hong Kong after it reverts from British to Chinese rule next year, Shen said Hong Kong would enjoy a large measure of autonomy. Beijing would be unable to interfere in the day-to-day running of the territory except in the areas of foreign relations and national defence.
Shen added that Taiwan would enjoy an even greater measure of autonomy when it was "peacefully reunited with the motherland".
